extracted.intended_audience: CVPR 2018 reviewers (conference paper reviewers in computer vision / machine learning)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for reviewing papers submitted to CVPR 2018: how to evaluate submissions, write constructive reviews, follow ethical/conflict rules, and use the CMT reviewing system. Focused on assigning scores, writing text reviews, handling rebuttals, and procedural checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind reviews / anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors were asked to take reasonable efforts to hide their identities; reviewers should also make all efforts to keep their identity invisible to the authors. Reviewers should not search for the authors of a paper, and complain that the paper is not anonymous if they happen to find them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Author Guidelines for details on anonymization and referencing one's prior work. If you know authors via arXiv you should still review independently as if arXiv didn't exist. Avoid using 'you' (address authors as 'the authors' or 'the paper'). Do not ask authors to cite your papers (this can reveal identity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as you get your reviewing assignment, go through all the papers to make sure there is no obvious conflict with you and you feel comfortable reviewing the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a conflict exists, email the Program Chairs immediately. Conflicts include (but are not limited to): same institution as an author; direct involvement in the work; membership on the author's thesis committee; collaboration in the past three years; advisor/advisee relationships. If you recognize a paper and feel it could present a conflict, return it rather than submit a review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect confidentiality / protect ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect the confidentiality of the ideas represented in the papers you review; submissions are not published documents and may be proprietary or still in development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not show the paper, results, videos/images, or supplementary material to anyone except those you have asked to help write the review. Do not use ideas from the paper to develop new ones. After the review process, destroy copies of papers and supplementary material and erase any implementations or results written to evaluate the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts and impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be absolutely no question about the impartiality of any review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If assigned a paper where your review would create a possible conflict of interest, return the paper and not submit a review. Use judgment about borderline cases but err on the side of avoiding perceived conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be professional and courteous
rubrics_metrics.description: Belittling or sarcastic comments have no place in the reviewing process. Write a courteous, informative, incisive, and helpful review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone is important: word criticisms diplomatically while staying true to your thoughts. Write as if providing feedback to a respected colleague who wants your opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to look for: novelty and potential impact
rubrics_metrics.description: CVPR is looking for new ideas. Reviewers should look for what's good or stimulating in the paper and embrace novel, brave concepts even if they have not been tested on many datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh both the novelty and potential impact of the work alongside the reported performance. A method not exceeding state-of-the-art accuracy on a benchmark is not grounds for rejection by itself. Each accepted paper should be technically sound and make a contribution to the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepted papers should be technically sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check correctness of methods, results, assumptions, and claims; point out methodological flaws and suggest fixes. Technical soundness is a core acceptance criterion alongside novelty and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance is not sole criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance and rejection decisions should not be determined solely by the method's raw performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject solely because a method does not beat the state of the art. Similarly, do not accept solely because it outperforms an arXiv paper. Consider novelty, insight, and potential impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific and detailed in reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Your main critique should be written as a list of strengths and weaknesses of the paper. Use bullet points and explain your arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short reviews are unhelpful. Provide specific citations when claiming something is well known or previously done. Explain precisely how prior work relates. Include actionable suggestions to help authors improve the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constructive suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include specific feedback on ways the authors can improve their papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions can be very specific (e.g., recommend a numerical solver) or general (suggest a new dataset or application). Be generous about giving new ideas. Your review should help authors and also inform Area Chairs and other reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful about inventing policy-based grounds for rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ad-hoc policy innovations in reviews that are not CVPR policy (e.g., rejecting for non-public datasets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reviewer invents a new policy requirement (such as data must be public), that's unfair. Refer to existing CVPR policies (e.g., double submission, plagiarism) rather than creating new ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity about novelty claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a submitted work 'has been done before' must be backed up with specific references and an explanation of how closely they are related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For positive reviews, summarize which novel aspects are most interesting. If you assert similarity to prior work provide citations and concrete argumentation; otherwise authors and ACs cannot act on vague assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of arXiv and non-peer-reviewed reports
rubrics_metrics.description: ArXiv papers are not considered prior work since they have not been peer reviewed; citations to arXiv/technical reports are not required and missing them is not grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is Not OK to accept/reject solely because of arXiv comparisons or to treat arXiv as the state of the art. It is OK to suggest authors acknowledge an arXiv paper, and OK for authors to decline to acknowledge it. If concerned about plagiarism with arXiv, raise it in confidential comments to the Area Chair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual / double submission policy
rubrics_metrics.description: By submitting to CVPR authors acknowledge their manuscript has not been previously published or accepted for publication in substantially similar form and is not under review elsewhere during the review period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication is defined as a written work longer than four pages that was submitted for peer review and accepted. arXiv and technical reports without peer review are not considered publications. As a rule of thumb, CVPR submission should contain no more than 20% material from previous publications. Contact Program Chairs for borderline cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism consists of appropriating the words or results of another without credit. Reviewers can generally recognize plagiarism and should refer suspected cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspected plagiarism cases will be referred to the IEEE Intellectual Property office, which handles procedures and penalties. If unsure, raise concerns in confidential comments to the Area Chair and specify evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate each paper on its own (no quotas)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no minimum number of papers you should accept or reject; each paper should be evaluated in its own right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume your stack should match the overall conference acceptance rate. If most papers you review have value, accept them; if rejecting many, provide clear and very specific comments in each review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid revealing identity / self-citation avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't give away your identity by asking the authors to cite several of your own papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid recommending citation of your own work unless genuinely necessary and disclosed through proper channels. Use neutral phrasing and avoid directing authors to cite specific personal works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reviewer workflow and CMT usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps for using the CMT reviewer system: download assigned papers, check conflicts/violations, familiarize with 'Detailed Reviews and Discussions', add and submit reviews, optionally review offline, and verify uploads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure browser cookies/Javascript enabled; do not create a new CMT account; add cmt@microsoft.com to safe senders; saving a draft is private; 'Submit' makes it visible to Area Chair and requires all required items filled. Offline review templates can be downloaded/edited and uploaded (verify after upload).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for submission rule violations
rubrics_metrics.description: When downloading papers, check for possible conflicts or submission rule violations and notify Program Chairs immediately if found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of violations: over 8 pages (not including references); constitutes a double submission; supplementary material includes a newer version of the paper; plagiarism. Specify exact nature of violation when reporting. Refer to Author Guidelines for details on dual submission and other policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in post-rebuttal discussions and finalize recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: After the rebuttal period, reviewers should work with Area Chairs to clear up confusions and attempt to reach consensus on papers. Enter your final recommendation after considering rebuttal and discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary ratings may change; final recommendation should reflect judgment after reading authors' rebuttal and participating in any discussion. Use the CMT discussion/bulletin board feature when Area Chairs post notes.
